transcript.text: summary-claude 发现了什么？给我讲讲输入层的硬编码规则是怎么回事。

summary-claude 找到了。 输入层里有大约一千五百个字符的手写规则，靠关键词把「好的」「继续」「yes」「等一下」这类短回复直接变成批准或取消，完全不问模型。 它觉得这是问题。 一句话里如果带着条件，会被整句丢掉：有人说过「好的继续，不过先跑测试」，系统只看到前半句就立刻批准了，后半句根本没送到模型。 而且这样的词表有三份，彼此还不一致，同一个词在一份里算批准，在另一份里不算。 测试里也有相当一部分只是在测这些词表。 要我让它动手改吗？ Options: 改，删掉词表保留安全规则; 先不改.
然后呢？
接下来就是动手改这一步。 summary-claude 会删掉那三份词表，把每条回复都交给模型判断，同时保留拒绝危险按键的那条安全规则，然后跑一遍测试。 代价是普通一句「是」会多等一秒多。 我建议就让它改。 要我让它开始吗？ Options: 让它改; 先不改.
你可以给我一点详细的解释吗？

那我把这件事说细一点。 输入层是系统在把你的话交给模型之前，先自己看一眼的那一层。 它现在没有真的去理解，而是拿着三份手写的词表去对：一份列批准类的话，比如「好的」「继续」「行」「yes」 一份列拒绝类的话。 一份列「先等等」类的话，比如「等一下」「先不要」。 对上哪一个，它就自己按下对应的键，根本不问模型。 麻烦在于它对上的是整句话里的几个字，不是你的意思。 有人说过「好的继续，不过先跑测试」，它只看到「好的继续」就批了，后半句没人看见。 要我让它开始改吗？ Options: 让它改; 先不改.
为什么这是个问题？

因为这一层是在替你做决定。 它不等模型看懂你的意思，看到那几个字就直接替你按下批准或者取消。 所以会出两种事。 一是你说了条件，条件被丢掉：你说「好的，不过先跑测试」，它只听见前半句就批了，你的附加要求从没被看到。 二是同一个说法在不同地方结果不一样，因为三份词表各写各的，你没法预料它这次会怎么判。 还有一层是测试也在测这些词表，等于在测错的东西，真正的行为反而没人看着。 要我让它开始改吗？ Options: 让它改; 先不改.
举个例子？

举个最清楚的。 你和它说话时写成「好的，继续，不过先别动数据库」，这句话里批准和限制都在。 程序看到「好的，继续」这三个字就当场按了批准，后面那句「先别动数据库」它没读到，也就没有传下去。 反过来也一样：你说「不行，先等一下再决定」，它可能先看到「不行」就按了取消，而你其实是想让它停下来等你。 同一个说法在不同地方结果还会不一样，因为三份词表各写各的，比如「行吧」在一份里算同意，在另一份里就不算，它这次算不算全看走的是哪条路。 要我让它开始改吗？ Options: 让它改; 先不改.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: The CEO's goal was: "understand what the hard-coded rules in the input layer are, why they are a problem, and what can be done, in enough detail to decide". By the end of the call, did the CEO get what they asked for: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

transcript.text: What did bench-codex find about the flaky test? Explain it to me.

Codex found the flaky test fails about one run in twelve. The test fires its request before the price cache has finished warming up, so the calculation sometimes reads an empty cache and charges full list price, which drops the member discount. It is a test problem, not a bug in the product: in production the cache is warm before any customer arrives. Codex has two fixes in mind and recommends the first, a small change that makes the test wait for the cache to be ready. The other replaces the cache with a stand-in for the test, which it says hides the very path that was flaking. Shall I have Codex put in the first fix? Options: Fix one, wait for the cache; Fix two, use a stand-in cache.
Then?

Nothing has moved since a moment ago. Codex is idle and still has not touched the code, and the only thing waiting is your call on which of its two fixes to try. I would take the first, the three line change that makes the test wait for the cache. Shall I have Codex put in that first fix? Options: Fix one, wait for the cache; Fix two, use a stand-in cache.
More detail please.

Here is the whole of it. Codex ran the flaky test many times in a row and saw it fail several times on its own, with no code changing in between. It traced the cause: the test fires its request before the price cache has finished warming up, so when the test loses that race the calculation reads an empty cache, falls back to list prices, and misses the member discount, which is why the total comes out higher than expected. That same flakiness blocked two deploys last week, and each one needed a quarter of an hour or so of hand re-running to get past it. Shall I have Codex put in the first fix? Options: Fix one, wait for the cache; Fix two, use a stand-in cache.
Why does that happen?

Because the test starts two things at once instead of one after the other. It kicks off the cache warm-up and, in the same breath, sends the request that needs the cache. On a quiet machine the warm-up finishes first and the test passes. On a busy one the request wins the race and the test fails. Codex saw exactly that: same code, same test, different outcome depending on how loaded the machine was. Since nothing in the test forces an order, the result is a coin toss, and that is why it blocks deploys at random. Shall I have Codex put in the first fix, the one that makes the test wait for the cache? Options: Fix one, wait for the cache; Fix two, use a stand-in cache.
Give me an example.

Think of a coffee counter. You order a pastry and the discounted member price, but the machine that holds the member prices is still starting up. If it is ready when you pay, you get the discount. If it is not, the till falls back to the price printed on the shelf and you pay full. Same order, same you, different price, only because of a second's difference in timing. Codex's test is the customer who sometimes reaches the till before the price machine is ready, and it fails for the same reason. Shall I have Codex put in the first fix, the one that makes the test wait for the cache? Options: Fix one, wait for the cache; Fix two, use a stand-in cache.

transcript.text: What did bench-codex find about the flaky test? Explain it to me.

bench-codex found the flaky test is a test problem, not a real bug. The test fires its request before the price cache is warmed up, and when it loses that race the total comes back at full price instead of the discounted one. It fails about one run in twelve, and it has already cost two deploys last week, each needing a manual re-run. Shall I have it fix the test? Options: Wait for the cache to be ready in the test setup, its recommendation, 3 lines; Swap the cache for a fake in the test, more code but hides the warm-up path.
Then?

I didn't catch which you meant. Do you mean go ahead and have codex fix the failing test, or do you want to hear what happens after the fix? Options: Go ahead, have codex fix the test; Hold off, leave the code as it is; Tell me what would happen after the fix.
More detail please.

Here is the full picture from bench-codex. The test fails about one run in twelve. The cause is a race: the test sends its request before the price cache has warmed up, so the handler falls back to list prices and the total misses the member discount. That flake blocked two deploys last week, and each one needed a manual re-run. It says this is a test problem, not a production bug, because in production the cache warms up before the server takes traffic. It offered two fixes and recommends the first, waiting for the cache to be ready in the test setup. Shall I have codex fix it the first way? Options: Yes, fix it by waiting for the cache in the test setup; No, just tell me and leave it.
Why does that happen?

Because the test and the cache start at the same moment and the test gets there first. The server needs a short warm-up to fill its price list, and on most runs it wins, so the test sees the member price. One run in twelve it loses, the price list is still empty, so the test sees full price and fails. It is a timing coincidence, not something wrong with the shopping code. Shall I have codex fix it the recommended way, waiting for the cache to be ready before the test runs? Options: Yes, fix it the recommended way; No, leave it for now.
Give me an example.

Sure. Think of a shop opening at nine and the price board still being written up. A customer who walks in at nine sharp gets charged the shelf price instead of the members' price, because the board is not finished. Come in a moment later and you get the discount. The test is that customer arriving at nine sharp: seven times out of eighty four this week it got in before the board was ready and the total came out at full price. Shall I have codex fix it, so the test waits for the board to be ready? Options: Yes, fix it; No, leave it.

transcript.text: What did bench-codex find about the flaky test? Explain it to me.

bench-codex was asked to find out why the checkout test is flaky, and it found the answer. The test sends its request before the price cache has finished warming up, so the member discount sometimes gets missed and the total comes out wrong. It says this is a problem with the test, not with the real product, and it has not changed anything yet. Shall I have it apply the fix it recommends? Options: Have it do the recommended fix; Leave it for now.
Then?

Nothing has moved since a moment ago. Both workers are idle, and bench-codex is still waiting to hear whether you want it to go ahead with the fix. Shall I have it apply the fix it recommends? Options: Have it do the recommended fix; Leave it for now.
More detail please.

bench-codex ran the checkout test over and over and it failed in several of those runs, about one run in twelve. Here is its reading. The test fires off its request before the price cache has finished warming up. When the warm-up loses that race the request gets read from an empty cache and the member discount is dropped, so the total comes out at full price instead of the discounted one. This has been real cost, it blocked two deploys last week and each one needed a manual re-run of about twenty five minutes. Shall I have it apply the fix it recommends? Options: Have it do the recommended fix; Leave it for now.
Why does that happen?

bench-codex is digging into that now. I have sent it back into the code to trace exactly how the cache warms up and why the test sometimes reads it too early, and I will bring you the answer as soon as it comes back, about half a minute.
Give me an example.

A picture of it, not a found fact, since bench-codex is still tracing it. Think of a member buying something at a discount. The test sends off the order and then checks the total it gets back is the discounted one. When the price list has not finished loading in time, the discount step finds nothing to discount against, quietly leaves the total at full price, and the test sees full price where it expected the discount. That is a failure. In the runs where the price list did finish loading first, the same test sees the discounted total and passes.
